note: In Mark the priests simply promise Judas {mk 14:11 ἀργύριον} (“money”), and Mark gives no motive. Matthew has Judas ask the price and names it: {mt 26:15 τριάκοντα ἀργύρια} (“thirty silver pieces”), the wage paid to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah 11:12. Luke supplies a supernatural motive instead: {lk 22:3 Εἰσῆλθεν δὲ Σατανᾶς εἰς Ἰούδαν} (“Satan entered Judas”). John says the same, at the supper (13:27).

In the Synoptics the Last Supper is a Passover meal, {mk 14:12 ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον} (“when they sacrificed the Passover lamb”). The disciples are to look for {mk 14:13 ἄνθρωπος κεράμιον ὕδατος βαστάζων} (“a man carrying a water jar”), a recognizable sign since carrying water was usually women's work. Luke names the two disciples as {lk 22:8 Πέτρον καὶ Ἰωάννην} (“Peter and John”), the pair who lead the church together in Acts 3–4.

Mark's {mk 14:18 ὁ ἐσθίων μετ ἐμοῦ} (“one who is eating with me”) echoes Psalm 41:9. Only Matthew has Judas himself ask {mt 26:25 Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι ῥαββί} (“surely not I, Rabbi?”) and receive the enigmatic {mt 26:25 Σὺ εἶπας} (“you have said it”). Only John introduces the disciple {jn 13:23 ὃν ἠγάπα ὁ Ἰησοῦς} (“whom Jesus loved”). His scene closes with four words: {jn 13:30 ἦν δὲ νύξ} (“and it was **night**”).

Two traditions of the words over the cup. Mark and Matthew: {mk 14:24 τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς διαθήκης} (“my blood **of the covenant**”), echoing Exodus 24:8. Luke: {lk 22:20 ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου} (“the **new** covenant in my blood”), almost exactly Paul's wording in 1 Corinthians 11:25. Matthew alone adds {mt 26:28 εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν} (“for the forgiveness of sins”), a phrase he had removed from Mark's description of John's baptism.

Only Mark has the rooster crow **twice**: {mk 14:30 πρὶν ἢ δὶς ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι} (“before the rooster crows twice”). The other Gospels simplify to one crow. Luke's version is tender, and the Greek pronouns matter: Satan has demanded {lk 22:31 ὑμᾶς} (“you”, plural, all of you), but Jesus prayed {lk 22:32 περὶ σοῦ} (“for **you**”, singular, Peter). John places the prediction after the {jn 13:34 ἐντολὴν καινὴν} (“new commandment”).

A strange exchange found only in Luke. Jesus reverses his earlier mission instructions: {lk 22:36 ὁ μὴ ἔχων πωλησάτω τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀγορασάτω μάχαιραν} (“whoever has none should sell his cloak and buy a sword”), so that Isaiah 53:12 (“counted among the lawless”) is fulfilled. The disciples take him literally and produce two swords, and he replies {lk 22:38 Ἱκανόν ἐστιν}, either “that is enough” or, more likely, an exasperated “enough of this!”

Mark's Jesus is overwhelmed, {mk 14:33 ἤρξατο ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν} (“began to be distressed and agitated”), and prays in Aramaic: {mk 14:36 Αββα ὁ πατήρ}. Matthew has him fall {mt 26:39 ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ} (“on his face”). Luke's version is calmer, apart from the disputed verse about {lk 22:44 ὁ ἱδρὼς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος} (“his sweat like drops of blood”). John has no agony at all; only he calls the place {jn 18:1 κῆπος} (“a garden”).

Each Gospel adds something. Mark: a young man flees {mk 14:51 περιβεβλημένος σινδόνα ἐπὶ γυμνοῦ} (“wearing only a linen cloth”), a mystery that has produced many theories. Matthew: {mt 26:52 πάντες γὰρ οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀπολοῦνται} (“all who take the sword will perish by the sword”). Luke: Jesus {lk 22:51 ἁψάμενος τοῦ ὠτίου ἰάσατο αὐτόν} (“touched the ear and healed him”). John: the soldiers fall back at {jn 18:6 Ἐγώ εἰμι} (“I am”), and only John names Peter as the swordsman and the servant as Malchus.

Mark's Jesus answers the high priest plainly: {mk 14:62 Ἐγώ εἰμι} (“I am”). Matthew's answer is evasive, {mt 26:64 Σὺ εἶπας} (“you have said so”), and so is Luke's. The famous minor agreement comes next. Mark's guards blindfold Jesus and say only “Prophesy!”. Matthew and Luke **both** add the same five words: {mt 26:68 τίς ἐστιν ὁ παίσας σε} and {lk 22:64 τίς ἐστιν ὁ παίσας σε} (“Who is it that struck you?”). In Matthew, where there is no blindfold, the taunt makes little sense.

Matthew explains why Peter is recognized: {mt 26:73 ἡ λαλιά σου δῆλόν σε ποιεῖ} (“your **accent** gives you away”), a Galilean speaking in Jerusalem. Only Luke records that at the rooster's crow {lk 22:61 στραφεὶς ὁ κύριος ἐνέβλεψεν τῷ Πέτρῳ} (“the Lord turned and looked at Peter”). John's third questioner is {jn 18:26 συγγενὴς ὢν οὗ ἀπέκοψεν Πέτρος τὸ ὠτίον} (“a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off”).

A brief transition with almost no shared wording outside Mark–Matthew. Mark: {mk 15:1 εὐθὺς πρωῒ} (“at once, early”) the council binds Jesus and hands him over. John adds a detail that sets his chronology apart. The accusers would not enter the governor's residence {jn 18:28 ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν ἀλλὰ φάγωσιν τὸ πάσχα} (“so as not to be defiled, but to eat the Passover”). In John, then, the Passover meal has not yet happened.

Only Matthew tells this: Judas {mt 27:3 μεταμεληθεὶς} (“seized with remorse”) returns the money and {mt 27:5 ἀπήγξατο} (“hanged himself”). Acts 1:18, by Luke, gives a different account: Judas buys a field himself and falls headlong. Matthew attributes his scripture to {mt 27:9 Ἰερεμίου τοῦ προφήτου} (“Jeremiah the prophet”), though the words come mainly from Zechariah 11:12–13, blended with Jeremiah's potter and field purchase.

Pilate's question is word for word the same in all four Gospels: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Mark's Jesus replies {mk 15:2 Σὺ λέγεις} (“you say so”). Luke frames the trial with three explicitly political charges ({lk 23:2 κωλύοντα φόρους Καίσαρι διδόναι}, “forbidding tribute to Caesar”) and three verdicts of innocence, the first {lk 23:4 Οὐδὲν εὑρίσκω αἴτιον} (“I find no guilt”). John turns it into a dialogue, ending in {jn 18:38 Τί ἐστιν ἀλήθεια} (“what is truth?”).

Only Luke has Pilate send Jesus to Herod Antipas, who is in Jerusalem for the festival. Herod {lk 23:8 ἐχάρη λίαν} (“was very glad”), because he had long wanted to see a sign, a wish Luke planted at 9:9. Jesus says nothing. The scene ends with a bitter aside: {lk 23:12 ἐγένοντο δὲ φίλοι ὅ τε Ἡρῴδης καὶ ὁ Πιλᾶτος} (“Herod and Pilate became friends that day”). In Acts 4:27 the church reads Psalm 2 as fulfilled by this alliance.

In Matthew Pilate offers a choice between two men named Jesus: {mt 27:17 Ἰησοῦν τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἢ Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον χριστόν} (“Jesus Barabbas or Jesus called Christ”). Barabbas means “son of the father” in Aramaic. Most manuscripts lack the first “Jesus”, but modern editions print it. Only Matthew has Pilate's wife's dream and the hand-washing, followed by {mt 27:25 Τὸ αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐφ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν} (“his blood be on us and our children”), a line later used catastrophically to justify persecuting Jews.

Mark's soldiers dress Jesus in {mk 15:17 πορφύραν} (“purple”), the imperial color, and Matthew in a soldier's scarlet cloak. They parody the salute to the emperor (*Ave Caesar*) with {mk 15:18 Χαῖρε βασιλεῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων} (“Hail, King of the Jews!”). Luke omits this scene but has Herod's soldiers mock Jesus earlier (23:11). John moves the mockery into the middle of the trial.

Mark identifies Simon of Cyrene as {mk 15:21 τὸν πατέρα Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Ῥούφου} (“the father of Alexander and Rufus”), apparently men his readers knew. The soldiers {mk 15:21 ἀγγαρεύουσιν} (“press into service”) him, a Persian loanword for compulsory service also used in Matthew 5:41. Only Luke has Jesus address the mourning women: {lk 23:28 Θυγατέρες Ἰερουσαλήμ μὴ κλαίετε ἐπ ἐμέ} (“daughters of Jerusalem, don't weep for me”). In John, Jesus carries the cross himself.

Mark gives a time: {mk 15:25 Ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη} (“it was the third hour”, about 9 a.m.). John has Pilate's trial still going at about the sixth hour (noon). The charge differs slightly in each Gospel. John says it was written {jn 19:20 Ἑβραϊστί Ῥωμαϊστί Ἑλληνιστί} (“in Hebrew, Latin and Greek”). Only Luke has the penitent criminal and the promise {lk 23:43 σήμερον μετ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ} (“today you will be with me in Paradise”).

Each Gospel gives Jesus different last words. Mark and Matthew: Psalm 22:1, {mk 15:34 Ἐλωῒ ἐλωῒ λεμὰ σαβαχθάνι}, in Aramaic, though Matthew's {mt 27:46 Ἠλὶ ἠλὶ} is Hebrew, which makes the bystanders' confusion with “Elijah” more natural. Luke has Psalm 31:5, {lk 23:46 Πάτερ εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου} (“into your hands I commit my spirit”). John: {jn 19:30 Τετέλεσται} (“it is finished”). Mark's centurion says “Son of God”; Luke's says {lk 23:47 δίκαιος} (“innocent/righteous”).

Mark's Joseph of Arimathea is {mk 15:43 εὐσχήμων βουλευτής} (“a respected council member”) who {mk 15:43 τολμήσας} (“took courage”) to ask for the body. Luke's tomb is one {lk 23:53 οὗ οὐκ ἦν οὐδεὶς οὔπω κείμενος} (“where no one had yet been laid”), echoing the colt no one had yet ridden. In John, Nicodemus brings {jn 19:39 ὡς λίτρας ἑκατόν} (“about a hundred pounds”) of myrrh and aloes, roughly 33 kg, a quantity fit for a king.

Only Matthew has the chief priests ask Pilate to secure the tomb, {mt 27:64 μήποτε ἐλθόντες οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ κλέψωσιν αὐτὸν} (“lest his disciples come and steal him”). Pilate replies {mt 27:65 Ἔχετε κουστωδίαν}, “you have a guard”, using a Latin loanword (*custodia*). The episode answers a rumor, still circulating when Matthew wrote, that the body had been stolen (see 28:15).

Mark's Gospel, in its earliest manuscripts, ends here, with the women fleeing and telling no one: {mk 16:8 ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ} (“for they were afraid”). Ending a sentence with *gar* is unusual, ending a book with it even more so. Matthew adds an earthquake and an angel who {mt 28:2 ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον} (“rolled away the stone”). Luke has {lk 24:4 ἄνδρες δύο} (“two men”), and the apostles dismiss the women's report as {lk 24:11 λῆρος} (“nonsense”). John adds a footrace between Peter and the Beloved Disciple.

Matthew's women meet Jesus on the road and {mt 28:9 ἐκράτησαν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας} (“took hold of his feet”). John's Mary Magdalene recognizes him only when he says her name, and answers {jn 20:16 Ραββουνι}. He then says {jn 20:17 Μή μου ἅπτου}, a present imperative better rendered “stop clinging to me” than the traditional “touch me not”. The longer ending of Mark describes Mary as the woman {mk 16:9 παρ ἧς ἐκβεβλήκει ἑπτὰ δαιμόνια} (“from whom he had cast out seven demons”), a detail drawn from Luke 8:2.

Only Matthew tells this. The guards are bribed to say {mt 28:13 Οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ νυκτὸς ἐλθόντες ἔκλεψαν αὐτὸν ἡμῶν κοιμωμένων} (“his disciples came by night and stole him while we slept”). Matthew adds a rare aside to his readers: the story {mt 28:15 διεφημίσθη ὁ λόγος οὗτος παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις μέχρι τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας} (“has been spread among Jews to this day”). In the next century, Justin Martyr also reports this counter-claim.

Only Luke tells this story in full. The two disciples' {lk 24:16 ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτῶν ἐκρατοῦντο} (“eyes were held”) until a meal, where Jesus repeats the four actions of the feeding and the Last Supper: {lk 24:30 λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον εὐλόγησεν καὶ κλάσας ἐπεδίδου} (“took the bread, blessed, broke, gave”). Mark's longer ending condenses it into one sentence, {mk 16:12 ἐφανερώθη ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ} (“he appeared in another form”), evidence that its author knew Luke.

Four very different scenes. Matthew's is on a mountain, and admits that {mt 28:17 οἱ δὲ ἐδίστασαν} (“some doubted”); it ends with {mt 28:20 ἐγὼ μεθ ὑμῶν εἰμι} (“I am with you”), which echoes “Emmanuel, God with us” (1:23). Luke insists on physical reality: {lk 24:39 σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα} (“flesh and bones”) and a piece of broiled fish. In John, Jesus {jn 20:22 ἐνεφύσησεν} (“breathed on”) them, the verb of Genesis 2:7 in the Septuagint. Mark's longer ending promises they will {mk 16:18 ὄφεις ἀροῦσιν} (“pick up snakes”).

Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus blessing the disciples and parting from them, and some manuscripts add {lk 24:51 καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν} (“and he was carried up into heaven”). Luke's Gospel seems to place this on Easter day itself; his second volume, Acts, places it forty days later. The longer ending of Mark adds that he {mk 16:19 ἐκάθισεν ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ} (“sat at the right hand of God”), the language of Psalm 110.
